translations.text: The Book of Judith
In the twelfth year of the reign of Nebuchadnezzar, king of Assyria, who reigned in Nineveh, the great city, in the days of Arphaxad, king of Media, who reigned in Ecbatana.
He built a tower for Ecbatana and surrounded it with a wall of cut stones. Each stone was three cubits wide and six cubits long, and the wall was seventy cubits high.
He built the towers at the gateway in the wall a hundred cubits high, and the gateway was sixty cubits wide.
He made gates and gateposts sixty cubits high and forty cubits wide, so that the chariots of his army could pass through.
In those days King Nebuchadnezzar made war against King Arphaxad in the plain, that is, the plain of Dura.

All the inhabitants of the mountain region and all who lived along the Euphrates, the Tigris, and the Ulai came out against him, in the plain of Arioch, king of Elam. Many nations gathered to fight against the Chaldeans.
Nebuchadnezzar, king of Assyria, sent word to all the inhabitants of Lebana, to all who lived in Cilicia, Damascus, Lebanon and its surrounding regions, and to all who lived along the sea.
and to the inhabitants of Carmel, Gilead, and Upper Galilee, and those in the great plain of Jezreel,

He also sent to everyone in Samaria and its cities, to those beyond the Jordan as far as Jerusalem, to those in Betane, Chelon, and Kadesh, to those along the river of Egypt, to those in Tahpanhes and Rameses, and to all Goshen as far as Zoan.
and to Memphis and all who lived in the land of Egypt, as far as the border of Cush.

All the inhabitants of the land rejected King Nebuchadnezzar’s words. They did not come to the war and were not afraid of him, because they were all united as one man. They sent his messengers back with their faces disgraced.

Nebuchadnezzar became very angry with this whole land. He swore by his throne and his kingdom that he would take revenge on all the territories of Cilicia, Damascus, and Bashan, kill with the sword all the inhabitants of Moab, the Ammonites, all Judah, and everyone in Egypt, and advance as far as the borders of both seas.
In the seventeenth year he prepared his army against King Arphaxad. He prevailed in battle and routed Arphaxad’s entire army, all his cavalry, and all his chariots.
He took control of his cities and reached Ecbatana. He captured the towers, plundered their open squares, and turned all their splendor into disgrace.
He captured Arphaxad in the mountains of Ragau, killed him on the heights, and destroyed him, to this day.
He returned to Nineveh with his army and a multitude of fighting men. There he boasted and feasted, he and his entire army, for one hundred and twenty days.
In the twenty-eighth year, on the twelfth day of the first month, a decision was made in the palace of King Nebuchadnezzar to take revenge on the whole land, as he had said.
He summoned all his servants and nobles and revealed to them the secret of his heart. And it happened, when he had finished speaking of harm against the whole land—
they too agreed to destroy all the people who had not obeyed the command of his mouth.
When they had reached agreement, Nebuchadnezzar, king of Assyria, summoned Holofernes, the commander of his army, because he was second in command, and said to him:

“This is what the great king, the lord of the whole earth, says: You are to go out from my presence and take with you one hundred and twenty thousand strong infantrymen and a great number of horses with their riders, twelve thousand in all.
Advance across the whole western land, against those who have disregarded the command of my mouth.

Tell them to prepare land and water for me, because I am coming against them in my anger. I will cover the face of the whole land with the infantry of my army and hand them over to the army as plunder.
Their valleys and ravines will be filled with their slain, and the river will overflow with their slain and be filled.
I will lead their captives to the ends of the earth.
Go out and seize all their territories for me. If they surrender, keep them for me until the day of their punishment.
As for those who refuse to submit, show them no pity, but hand them over to slaughter and the whole land to plunder.
For as I live, and by my kingdom, I have spoken, and I will do all these things with my own hands.
You must not disobey a single command of your lord. Instead, carry out in full what I have commanded you to do.”
Holofernes went out from his lord’s presence and summoned the nobles, the army commanders, and the officers of the Assyrian forces.
He mustered men chosen for war, as his lord had commanded him: one hundred and twenty thousand men and twelve thousand mounted archers.
He commanded them to assemble for battle.
He took a very great number of camels and donkeys to carry their provisions, and sheep, cattle, and flocks beyond counting for their food.
He also took a very large amount of gold and silver from the king’s treasury.
He and his army set out from Nineveh to march ahead of the king and cover the face of the whole western land with chariots and chosen infantry.
A great mixed crowd went out with them, like locusts and like the sand of the earth, and their total could not be counted.
He went out from Nineveh a three-day journey toward the plain of Bectileth. They camped opposite Bectileth, beside Mount Ange, to the north of Upper Cilicia.
He took his whole army—infantry, cavalry, and chariots—and set out from there into the mountains.
He devastated the people of Put and Lydia. They took captive all the descendants of Tiras, the descendants of Rameses, and the descendants of Ishmael who lived in the southern wilderness.
And [?] the land of the Chaldeans. He crossed the Euphrates and passed through southern Mesopotamia. He demolished all the fortified cities beside the Jabbok River, until they reached the sea.
They seized the territory of Cilicia, and he destroyed everyone who stood against him. He came to the southern territory of Japheth, facing all Arabia.
They surrounded all the Midianites, burned all their tents, and captured their encampments.

They went down to the fields of Damascus during the wheat harvest. They burned all their fields and devastated their plain and the grazing grounds of their sheep. They destroyed their cattle and their herds, plundered their cities, and killed their young men with the sword.

Fear and trembling fell on everyone living along the sea, in Tyre and Sidon, on the inhabitants of Sur, on everyone living in Lebana, and on the inhabitants of Ashdod, Ashkelon, and Gaza. They were very afraid of him.
They sent messengers to him with words of peace, saying:
They said, “We are servants of Nebuchadnezzar, the great king. Here we stand before you. Do with us whatever seems good to you.”
“Here before you are all the land where we live, all our fields and grain-bearing plains, our sheep and cattle, and every dwelling place of our livestock. Do with us whatever seems good to you.”
Our towns and their inhabitants are your servants. Come and deal with us as you see fit.”
The messengers came and spoke these words to Holofernes.
He and his army went down to the cities along the sea. He stationed garrisons in the fortified cities and took from them auxiliary troops of chosen men.
The towns and villages welcomed him with garlands, [?], and tambourines.

He demolished all their temples, and they cut down all their objects of worship, because he had secretly given orders to destroy all the gods of the earth, so that all peoples and languages would serve and worship Nebuchadnezzar himself and call him a god.
And he came to Jezreel, beside Dothan, opposite the great pass of Judea.
He camped between Geba and Beth-shean and spent a month there putting all the affairs of his army in order.

The Israelites living in Judea heard everything that Holofernes, the commander of the army of Nebuchadnezzar, king of Assyria, had done among the nations, and how they had taken their gods and handed them over to destruction.
They were greatly afraid of him and were alarmed for Jerusalem and for the temple of the Lord their God.

For they had only recently returned from captivity, and the Jewish people had only recently been gathered together. The sacred vessels and the altar had only recently been consecrated after their defilement.
They sent word to the territory of Samaria, to the villages of Beth-horon, to Abel-meholah, to Jericho, to Kikkar, to Beth-horon, and to the valley of Gallim.
They occupied all the high mountain peaks, fortified the villages on them, and equipped them for war, since their lands had only recently been harvested.
Eliakim, who was high priest in Jerusalem in those days, wrote to the inhabitants of Bethulia and Betomesthaim, which is above Masra, opposite Jezreel and facing the great plain beside Dothan.
He said, “Hold the mountain pass, for that is the entrance into Judea.” It was not easy for those coming up, because the ascent was narrow even for two men together.
The Israelites did as Eliakim the high priest and the elders of all the people of Israel who lived in Jerusalem had instructed.
All Israel cried out to the Lord with all their heart and humbled themselves with a solemn fast.
They, their wives, their children, every resident, every hired worker, and every slave bought with silver tied sackcloth around their waists.
Every Israelite man, woman, and child living in Jerusalem fell facedown before the temple of the Lord, and they wrapped the altar in sackcloth.

Together they cried out to the God of Israel not to give their children over to plunder, their wives to captivity, their cities to destruction, or the sanctuary to defilement and disgrace, to the delight of the nations.
The Lord heard and saw their afflictions. The people fasted for many days throughout Judea and in Jerusalem, and they fell down before the sanctuary of the mighty Lord.

Eliakim the high priest and all who served before the Lord, the priests and ministers, had sackcloth tied around their waists as they offered the regular whole burnt offerings, the votive offerings, the dedicated gifts, and the offerings of the people.
Ashes were put on their turbans, and they cried out to the Lord with all their strength to look favorably upon the whole house of Israel.

Holofernes, the commander of the Assyrian army, was told that the Israelites had assembled for battle, occupied the mountain pass, fortified all the high mountain peaks, and set ambushes in the fields.
Holofernes became very angry. He summoned all the nobles of Moab, the rulers of the Ammonites, and all the leaders of the coastal cities.

He said to them, “Tell me, Canaanites, who are these people who live in the mountains? What are their cities, and how large is their army? What is their military strength and power? Who is the leader who rules over them?”
“And why have they refused to come out to meet me, unlike all those who live in the caves?”

Achior, the leader of the Ammonites, said to him, “Let my lord listen to the words of his servant. I will tell you the truth about the people who live near you in these mountains. No, no lying word will come from your servant’s mouth.
For these people are descended from the Chaldeans.
“They first lived in Mesopotamia, because they were unwilling to follow the gods of their ancestors, who were honored in the land of the Chaldeans.

“Instead, they turned away from their ancestors’ gods and worshiped the God of heaven, the God whom they knew. He drove them out from the presence of their gods, and they fled to Mesopotamia and lived there for many days.
“Their God told them to leave their ancestral homeland and go to the land of Canaan. They lived there and became rich in gold, silver, and very large herds of livestock.
“They went down to Egypt because of the famine that struck the land of Canaan. They settled there and were fed. They increased greatly there, and their families were beyond counting.
“The Egyptians rose against them and dealt cunningly with them. They enslaved them to work with clay and bricks, humbled the people, and made them slaves.
“They cried out to their God, and he struck the whole land of Egypt with incurable sores. The Egyptians drove them out of their land.
God dried up the Red Sea before them.
He brought them to the road to Mount Sinai and to Kadesh, and they drove out all the inhabitants of the desert.
“By their strength they destroyed everyone who lived in the land of the Amorites and the people of Heshbon. They crossed the Jordan and took possession of all the mountains.
“They drove out before them the Canaanites, Perizzites, Hivites, Jebusites, and all the Girgashites, and they lived there for many days.
“As long as they did not sin against their God, good things were with them, because he is a God who hates wrongdoing.

“But when they departed from the way he had commanded them to follow, they perished in many battles and were taken captive to a land that was not their own. Their God’s temple was trampled underfoot, and their city was captured by enemies.

“Now they have returned to their God and gathered from the places to which they were scattered. They have regained control of Jerusalem, where their sanctuary is, and have settled in the mountains that had been deserted.
“Now, my lord, if there is sin among these people and they are offending their God, let us consider that this will be a stumbling block for them, and let us go up and fight them.
“But if there is no wrongdoing among their people, let my lord pass them by. Otherwise their God may help them, and we will become a disgrace throughout the whole earth.”

When Achior finished speaking these words, all the people standing around the tent began to grumble. Holofernes’ nobles, the inhabitants of the coast, and the inhabitants of Moab said that Achior should be driven out.
For they said, “We are not afraid of the Israelites, for they are a people with no strength for battle.
So let us go up against them, and they will belong to your army, our lord Holofernes.”
When the uproar of the men surrounding them had subsided, Holofernes, the commander of the Assyrian army, said to Achior in front of all the people:

“Who are you, Achior, and all the Moabites and the hired men of Ammon, that you have prophesied to us as you have today? You told us not to fight the people of Israel because their God helps them. Who is God except Nebuchadnezzar, king of the whole earth?

“He will send his army and destroy them from the face of the earth, and their God will not rescue them. We, Nebuchadnezzar’s servants, will strike them down as though they were a single man. They will not withstand the neighing of our horses.

“For we will destroy them. Their lands will be drenched with their blood, and their plains will be filled with their corpses. Not even a footprint of theirs will remain before us. They will be utterly destroyed, says Nebuchadnezzar, lord of the whole earth, and his words will not be revoked.
“But you, Achior, a hired man of Ammon, who have spoken these words—on the day of your wrongdoing, you will not see [?] from today until I take vengeance on the people who came up from Egypt.
“Then the sword of my army and the spear of my servants will pierce your side, and you will fall among their slain when I return.
My servants will take you away today and leave you in one of the cities of Israel.
You will not die until you perish with them today.
“For you thought in your heart that they could not be captured. Your face will not see you in prosperity [?]. For I have spoken, and not one of my words will fail.”
Holofernes ordered the servants attending him in his tent to seize Achior, take him to Bethulia, and hand him over to the Israelites.
A man seized him and brought him outside the army's camp. He took him to the mountain, and they went to the spring of water below the city.
When the men of the city saw them, they took their weapons and went outside the city to the mountaintop, every man who could use a sling. They secured the ascent and slung stones at them.
They withdrew from there, tied Achior up, and left him lying at the foot of the mountain. Then they went back to their master.
The Israelites came down from the city, stood over him, and untied him. They brought him up to the city and took him to their city's leaders.
In those days these were Uzziah son of Micah, from the tribe of Simeon; Chabris son of Othniel; and Charmi son of Mishael.
They summoned the city's elders, and all their young men, women, and children hurried to the assembly. They stood Achior in the midst of all the people, and Uzziah asked him what had happened.
He answered and told them everything Holofernes's people had said, everything he himself had said before the Assyrian leaders, and how Holofernes had boasted against the house of Israel.
All the people fell facedown, worshiped God, and said:
Lord, God of heaven, look upon their arrogance and have mercy on the humiliation of your people. Look upon your sanctuary this day.
They comforted Achior and praised him highly.
Uzziah took him away from the assembly and brought him to his house. He made room for the elders and called upon the God of Israel all night to help them.
The next day Holofernes ordered his entire army and all who had come with him to help him to march against Bethulia, seize all the mountain ascents, and wage war against the Israelites.

That day all the men and their entire army set out: one hundred seventy-two thousand men and twenty-two thousand cavalry, besides their baggage and the very large number of people who accompanied them.
They camped in the valley beside the city, by the spring of water. The camp stretched in width from Routhim to Abel-meholah, and in length as far as Karmon, opposite Jezreel.

When the Israelites saw how numerous they were, they were greatly alarmed and said to one another, “Now neither the whole surface of the earth, nor the high mountains, nor the hills can bear their weight.”
Each man took his weapons of war. They lit fires on the towers of their walls and kept watch throughout that night.
On the second day Holofernes brought out his entire army against the Israelites living in Bethulia.
They explored the ascent to the city, went to the springs of water, and seized them. They assigned them to all the companies of warriors, and he returned to his people.
All the leaders of the descendants of Esau and all the rulers of Moab, the chiefs of the city beside the sea, approached him and said to him:
“Let our lord listen to this advice, so that your army will not suffer defeat.
“This people does not rely on spears. Instead, they rely on the height of the mountains where they live, because it is not easy to approach the mountaintops.
So now, our lord, do not fight them in a regular battle, and not a man of your people will fall.
But remain in your camp and keep all the men of your army there. Let your servants seize the spring of water that flows from beneath the foot of the mountain.

For all the inhabitants of Bethulia draw water from there. Thirst will destroy them, and they will surrender their cities. We who are with you will go up to the nearby mountaintops and camp on them. They will be kept under watch so that not a single person can leave the city.
They will perish from hunger and thirst, together with their wives and children, until the sword comes upon them and they fall in the streets.”
You will repay them severely for spurning you and not coming out to meet you in peace.”
Their words pleased Holofernes and all his servants, and he ordered that what they had proposed be done.
The Moabite force set out, accompanied by five thousand Assyrian infantry. They camped in the valley and seized the Israelites' waters and springs.

The descendants of Esau and the Ammonites went up, accompanied by twelve thousand Assyrians, and camped on the mountain opposite Routhim. Some of them camped to the south and east, opposite Akraboth, which faces Cush, on the Peor stream. The rest of the Assyrian army camped on the plain and covered the face of the earth. Their tents and equipment, spread out among them, were very numerous.
The Israelites cried out to their God, and their spirits were distressed, because their enemies had surrounded them and there was no way to escape from among them.
The Assyrian armies—infantry, chariots, and cavalry—remained camped around them for two months and four days. The inhabitants of Bethulia emptied their water cisterns.

Their water jars were emptied, and they had no water left to drink. Their children and wives were fainting, because they had no water left to drink their fill even for one day, since water was being rationed to them.
Their children, wives, and troops grew very faint and were dying of thirst. They fell in the streets of the cities and at the entrances to the gates, with no strength left in them.
The young men, women, and children gathered against Uzziah and the city's leaders. They cried out loudly and said in the presence of the elders:
“May the Lord judge between us and you, because you have done us a great wrong by not negotiating peace with the Assyrians.
Now we have no one to help us. Instead, the Lord has handed us over through you, to perish before them from thirst and in utter destruction.
Now summon them and surrender the city to them, to Holofernes' people and his whole army, to be taken captive and plundered.
For it is better for us to become their male and female slaves and stay alive than to see with our own eyes the death of our little children, our wives, and our sons as their lives waste away.
We call heaven and earth to witness against you, and the Lord, the God of our ancestors, who is exacting punishment from us according to our sins, that you must act on these words this very day.”
There was weeping throughout the assembly, and they all cried out together in a loud voice to the Lord God.
Uzziah said to them, “Take courage, my brothers, and let us endure another five days. Perhaps the Lord God will turn his mercy toward us, for he will not abandon us completely.”
But if five days pass and no help comes to us, we will do as you have said.”
He sent the people away, each to his tent and to the city's walls and towers. He sent the women and children home. They were in very deep distress.

In those days Judith lived in the city. She was the daughter of Merari, daughter of Uz, son of Joseph, son of Uzziel, son of Elkanah, son of Hanan, son of Gibeon, son of Daphnin, son of Ahitub, son of Nain, son of Malchiah, son of Ir, son of Nethaniah, son of Shelumiel, son of Simeon, son of Israel.
Her husband Manasseh was from her own clan. He died during the barley harvest.

He had been overseeing the reapers in the field when the heat struck his head. He took to his bed and died in Bethulia, his city. They buried him with his ancestors in the field of Beth-ruthim and Beth-baalmon.
Judith lived as a widow in her house for three years and four months.
She made herself a shelter on the roof of her house, tied sackcloth around her waist, and wore her widow's clothes.
She fasted throughout her widowhood, except on Sabbaths, new moons, festivals, celebrations of renewal, and commemorations of the house of Israel.

She was beautiful to look at and lovely in appearance, wise at heart, good, and intelligent. She was also very rich, because her husband Manasseh had left her gold and silver, male and female slaves, livestock, and villages, and she managed them.
No one had anything bad to say about her, because she greatly feared God.

She heard the people's harsh words to the leader, because they were distressed by the shortage of water. Judith also heard everything Uzziah had said to them: he had listened to them and sworn to them that after five days they would surrender the city to the Assyrians.
She sent her maid, who was in charge of her storeroom, and summoned Uzziah, Chabris, and Charmis, the elders of the city.

They came to Judith, and she said to them, “Listen to me, inhabitants and inhabitants of Bethulia. What you said before the people today was not right. You established the oaths sworn between you and God, and said that you would surrender the city to our enemies unless the Lord our God turned to help us within that time.
Now who are you to put God to the test and make yourselves gods among human beings?
You are testing the purpose of the mighty Lord, which no one has ever known.

The depths of human hearts cannot be discovered, and the thoughts in their eyes cannot be grasped. How, then, can you comprehend God, who made all these things, or know his mind and understand his thoughts? No, my brothers, do not anger the Lord our God.
For if he does not choose to help us within five days, he has the power to protect us whenever he chooses and to shatter our enemies before us.
But you must not constrain the purpose of the Lord God. For God is not like a human being, to be exposed, nor like a mortal, to be diminished.
Instead, let us wait for his deliverance and call upon him to help us. If he wishes, he will hear our voice.
For no tribe, clan, people, or city among you has arisen in our generation or existed in our days that worships a god made by human hands, as happened in former days.
For this reason our ancestors were handed over to plunder and the sword, and suffered a great defeat before their enemies.
But we have known no god besides him, that he should turn his face away from our people.
For if we surrender, all Judea will surrender too. Our holy things will be plundered, and the Lord will hold us accountable with our blood for their defilement.

The slaughter of our brothers, the captivity of the land, and the defilement of our inheritance will fall back on our own heads among the nations where we will serve. We will become a stumbling block and a disgrace among all our captors.
For our enslavement will not bring us favor; instead, the Lord our God will make it a humiliation.
Now let us take responsibility for our brothers, because their lives depend on us, and the sanctuary, the temple, and the altar stand or fall with us.
Above all these things, let us please God, who is testing us as he tested our ancestors.
Remember everything he did with Abraham and Isaac, and everything that happened to Jacob in Mesopotamia while he was tending the sheep of Laban, his mother's brother.
He tested them to examine their hearts. Likewise, the Lord strikes us not for vengeance but for discipline, because we are close to him.
Uzziah said to her, “Everything you have said, you have said with a very good heart, and no one can oppose your counsel.
Your wisdom has not become known only today. From earlier days all the people have known your understanding, because the intentions of your heart are good.
But the people were very thirsty and forced us to do for them as we told them. They put us under an oath, and we cannot break it.
Now pray for us. Perhaps the Lord God will answer you, because you are a woman who fears God, and the Lord our God will send rain, so that our cisterns will be filled and we will not perish.
Judith said to them, “Listen to me. I will do something wise, and it will be remembered for generation after generation among our people.

You are to stand at the gate tonight, and I and my maidservant [?]. Within the days after which you said you would surrender the city to our enemies, the Lord will deliver Israel through my hands, by the means in which I am confident.”
But do not investigate what I am doing, because I will not reveal it to you until what I am doing is completed.”
Uzziah and the leaders said to her, “Go in peace. May the Lord go before you and avenge us on our enemies.”
They turned and went out of the shelter and returned to their homes.

Judith fell on her face, put ashes on her head, and tore her tunic, exposing the sackcloth she was wearing. At the very time when the evening incense was being offered in Jerusalem in the house of the Lord, Judith cried out to the Lord in a loud voice and said:

“Lord, God of my ancestor Simeon, you put a sword in his hand to take vengeance on the enemies who loosened a virgin's hair to defile her, uncovered her nakedness to shame her, and defiled her womb to disgrace her. For you had said that this must not happen.

For this reason you handed their leaders over to slaughter, and their bed, which had received the blood of your beloved. You struck down slaves together with their masters, and rulers together with their thrones.

They gave their wives over to captivity and their houses to plunder, and divided all their spoils among your beloved ones. They upheld your zeal, exposed the defilement of their blood, and called on you to help them. My God, hear me too, for I am a widow.
For you brought about the first things, the things in between, and also the things that came afterward. You intended them, and they came to be; you planned them,
and they stood before you. You called, and they said, ‘Here we stand.’ For all your ways are prepared, and your creation lay open before you.

Now the Assyrians have grown great in their strength. They have become proud of their horses and chariots. They boast of the might of their infantry, take pride in their swords, and trust in bows and slings. They do not know that you are the Lord who crushes wars.

The Lord is your name. Break their force, King of the ages, and crush their multitudes. Break their strength in your fury, because they have planned to defile the sanctuary where the glory of your name dwells, and to cast down the horns of your altar with iron.
Look at their arrogance, and send your wrath upon their heads. Give my hands, the hands of a widow, strength for what I have planned.
Through the deception of my lips, strike the man on the head; as for the ruler, break his strength by the hand of a woman.

For your power and strength do not depend on great numbers, nor are your gifts reserved for the mighty. Rather, you are the God of the humble, the helper of the lowly, the supporter of the weak, and the savior of the lost.
Yes, Lord, God of my ancestor and God of the inheritance of Israel, Lord of heaven and earth, creator of the waters, King of all creation, hear the voice of my prayer.

Make my cunning and deception bring death and injury to those who stand against your covenant, your holy temple, Mount Zion, and the land possessed by your children. For they have planned evil against us.
Make all the people and all generations know that you are the God of all power and all authority, and that there is no one who watches over Israel besides you.”
When Judith had finished crying out to the God of Israel and had completed all these words,
She rose from where she had been lying, called her maid, and went down to her house, where she stayed on Sabbaths and festivals.

She unfastened the sackcloth she was wearing and took off her widow’s clothes. She washed her mouth with water, anointed herself with choice oil, anointed the hair of her head, put sandals on her feet, and dressed in the fine clothes she used to wear during the lifetime of her husband Manasseh.
She put a headdress on her head and put on her bracelets, anklets, rings, earrings, and all her ornaments. She adorned herself lavishly, so as to catch the eyes of the men who saw her.
She gave her maid a skin of wine and a container of oil. She filled a bag with roasted flour, fig cakes, and bread, and put cheese in it. She packed her things and put them on her maid.
The two of them went out and came to the [?] of the city. There they found Uzziah and the elders of the city, Chabris and Charmis.
They saw the change in her appearance and the way she was dressed, and they were greatly amazed at her beauty. They said to her:
“May the God of our ancestors grant you mercy, and may you carry out your plan for the glory of the Israelites and the exaltation of Jerusalem.” She fell on her face and worshiped God.
She said to them, “Order the city gates to be opened, so that I may go out and fulfill the words you have spoken with me.” They ordered the young men to open the gate for her, as she had requested.
The people of the city did so, and Judith went out with her maid. The people of the city watched until she had gone down the mountain. When she came to the valley, they could no longer see her.
She went straight through the valley and encountered the first Assyrian guard post.

They seized her and questioned her, saying, “What is your business? Where have you come from, and where are you going?” She said to them, “I am a Hebrew woman, and I have fled from them, because they are about to be handed over to you to be devoured.”

“I have come to Holofernes, the commander of your army, to give him a truthful report and show him the road he should take. He will gain control of the whole hill country without losing a single human being, or even a breath of life.”
When the servants heard her words, they looked at her face, and her beauty was very remarkable in their eyes.
They said to her, “You have done well to save your life by hurrying down into our lord’s presence. Now go toward his tent. Some of our men will escort you until they hand you over to him.”
When you stand before him, do not be afraid in your heart. Instead, tell him what you have to say, and he will treat you well.”
They chose a hundred men from among themselves and entrusted her and her maid to them. They brought them to Holofernes’ tent.
There was a commotion throughout the camp, because those in the tents had heard of her arrival. They came and gathered around her as she stood outside Holofernes’ tent, until he was told about her.

They marveled at her beauty and welcomed her words because they were very good. Because of her, they were amazed at the Israelites, and they said to one another, “Who could despise a people who have women like these among them? Not one of them should be left alive, or those who survive will outwit the whole world.”
All Holofernes’ soldiers and all his servants came out, and they brought her into the tent.
Holofernes was lying at rest on his bed, beneath his canopy, which was woven with purple, gold, emeralds, and precious stones.
They told him about her. When he heard, he went out into the courtyard of the tent, with silver lamps burning before him, and they brought her in to him.
When Judith stood before him and his servants, they were all amazed at the beauty of her face. She fell on her face and bowed before him, but his servants took hold of her and raised her up.
Holofernes said to her, “Take courage, woman. Do not be afraid in your heart, for I have harmed no one who is willing to serve Nebuchadnezzar, king of the whole earth.”
“Even now, if your people who live in the hill country had not rejected me, I would not have raised a spear against them. They have brought these things on themselves.”
“Now tell me why you fled from them and came to us. You have come to safety. Take courage: from this night onward you will live.”
For no one will harm you, and I will treat you as my lord’s servants are treated.”
Judith said to him, “Listen to the words of your servant, and let your servant speak before you. I will tell you no lies tonight.”
“If you listen to my words, everything will be delivered into your hands—all that God will accomplish with you. My lord will not fail in his plans as long as he lives.”

“For as surely as Nebuchadnezzar, king of the whole earth, lives, not only will human beings serve him because of you, but wild animals, livestock, and the birds of the sky will also acknowledge Nebuchadnezzar through your power.”
“We have heard of your wisdom and the skill of your mind. It is said throughout the earth that you alone are the best in the whole kingdom, remarkable in knowledge and mighty in battle.”
And now, my lord, concerning what Achior said in the assembly before you: we have heard his words, because the people of the city received him, and he told them everything he had said before you.

Therefore, my lord, do not disregard his words, but take them to heart, because they are true. Our people cannot be punished, nor can the sword prevail against them, unless they sin against their God.
And now, so that my lord may not be without success, death has fallen upon them, and a great sin has overtaken them. By committing it, they will provoke their God to anger.
Because their provisions have run short and their water has run out, they have decided to slaughter their livestock and eat everything that their God, in his laws, commanded them not to eat.

They have decided to eat the firstfruits of the grain, wine, and oil, all of which they had reserved as sacred offerings for the priests who stand before God in Jerusalem. They want to eat things that no one among the people is permitted even to touch with their hands.
They have also sent to Jerusalem, to those who carried their message to the elders, because the inhabitants there have also done all these things.
When they send word back to them and they do this, they will be handed over to you that very day, and you will destroy them.
For this reason I, your servant, fled from them when I saw these things. God sent me to accomplish something with you that will astonish the whole earth—all who hear about it.

For your servant fears God and worships before the God of heaven day and night. Now I will stay with you, my lord, but your servant will go out at night to the valley. I will pray to God, and he will show me when they are committing their sins.
And I will come and make it known to you. You will march out with your army, and none of them will stand against you.

I will lead you through Judea until you reach Jerusalem, and I will set your throne in its midst. You will lead them like sheep without shepherds, and not a dog will bark at you. These things have been revealed to my mind, and I have been sent to tell you.
Her words pleased Holofernes and all his servants. They marveled at her beauty and wisdom, and said to her,
“From one end of the earth to the other, there is no woman like this, so beautiful in appearance and so intelligent in her words.”
Holofernes said to her, “God has done well to send you ahead of your people, so that honor may be remembered among us, while destruction comes upon those who despised my lord.

And now, you are beautiful in appearance and good in your understanding and your words. If you do as you have said, your God will be my God. You will live in the king’s palace, and your reputation will be more distinguished than that of anyone else in the whole earth.”
He ordered them to make preparations for her and to give her some of his dinner and some of the wine served at his drinking feast.
Judith said, “I will not eat any of it, lest it become a cause of sin for me. What I have brought with me will be enough for me.”
Holofernes said to her, “If it runs out, where will we get more of the same to give you? There is no one from your people here with us who has such food.”
Judith said, “As surely as you live, my lord, your servant will not finish what she has brought with her before God accomplishes through my hands what you have planned.”
Holofernes’ servants brought her into the tent. She slept until midnight and rose during the morning watch.
She sent word to Holofernes, saying, “Let my lord give orders that your servant be allowed to go out to pray.”
Holofernes ordered the guards not to stop her. She stayed in the camp for three days. At night she would go out to the valley of Bethulia and bathe in the spring.
When she came up, she would ask the God of Israel to direct her path toward the restoration of her people.
When she returned, she would remain in purity inside the tent until she took her food in the evening.
On the fourth day, Holofernes held a banquet for his servants alone. He invited none of the soldiers or officers.
He said to Bagoas, the eunuch who was in charge of everything he owned, “Go now and persuade that Hebrew woman who is with you to come to us and eat and drink with us.
It would be a disgrace for us to let a woman like this go without being intimate with her. If we do not seduce her, she will laugh at us.”

Bagoas went out from Holofernes, went in to her, and said, “Do not hesitate, beautiful young woman, to come before my lord and be honored in his presence. Drink wine with us and enjoy yourself. Today you will be honored like one of the daughters of the Assyrian nobles who serve in Nebuchadnezzar’s palace.”
Judith said to her, “Who am I to say no to my lord? I will eagerly do whatever pleases him, and this will be a source of pride to me until the day of my death.”

She got up and adorned herself with her clothes and all her womanly ornaments. Her maid went in and spread on the ground before Holofernes the lambskins she had received from Bagoas to sleep on, so that she could sit on them to eat.

Judith went in and sat down. Holofernes’ heart was stirred by her, and his soul was agitated, because he longed intensely to be with her. Ever since the day he saw her, he had been looking for an opportunity to have sexual relations with her.
Holofernes said to her, “Drink and enjoy yourself with us.”
Judith said, “I will drink, my lord, because today my life has been enriched far more than on any day I have lived.”
She took what her maid had prepared for her and ate it in his presence.
Holofernes delighted in her company and drank a great deal of wine, more than he had ever drunk on any day since his birth.

When evening came, his servants got up to leave. Bagoas closed the entrance of the tent from outside and sent away everyone who attended his master. Each went to his own tent, because they were exhausted by all the drinking that had taken place.
Judith was left alone in the tent, and Holofernes lay on his bed, overcome by wine.
Judith told her maid to stand outside the bedroom and wait for her to come out, as she did every day, because she had said, “I am going out to pray.” She had also said the same thing to Bagoas.

They all went away from there, and no one, great or small, remained in the bedroom. Judith stood beside Holofernes’ head and said, “Lord, Lord, God of all powers, look at this moment upon the work of my hands for the exaltation of Jerusalem.
For it is time to have compassion on your inheritance. Carry out the plans of my heart to crush the nations that have risen against us.”
She approached the bedpost beside Holofernes’ head and drew his sword.
She approached his bed, took hold of the hair of his head, and said, “Strengthen me today, God of Israel.”
She struck him twice on the neck with the sword and cut off his head.
She rolled his body off the bedding and took the canopy from the posts. Shortly afterward she went out and gave Holofernes’ head to her maid.

She put it in her food bag, and the two of them went out together, as they did at the time of prayer. They passed through the Assyrian camp, went around the whole of that valley, went up toward the city, and came to the gate.
Judith called to the guards from a distance, “Open the gate for me! Open it! For our God is with us. He has given Israel strength and power over their enemies, as he has today.”
When the people of the city heard her voice, they hurried to open their city gate for her and called the elders of the city.

They all ran, from the least to the greatest, because they were amazed that she had returned. They opened the gate and welcomed the two women. They lit a fire so that they could see and gathered around her.
She said to them in a loud voice, “Give thanks to the Lord our God, who has not withdrawn his mercy from Israel, but has crushed our enemies by our hands this night.”

She took the head out of the bag, showed it to them, and said, “Here is the head of Holofernes, the commander of the Assyrian army! And here is the canopy under which he lay in his drunkenness. The Lord has crushed him by the hand of a woman.
As surely as the Lord lives, who protected me on the way I traveled, my appearance led him astray, but he committed no sin with me through shameful defilement.”
All the people were utterly amazed. They fell down and worshiped the Lord, and all said together, “Blessed is the Lord our God, who today has crushed the enemies of his people!”

Uzziah said to her, “My daughter, you are blessed by God Most High above all the women on earth. And blessed is the Lord, who created heaven and earth, who guided you to take the head of the leader of our enemies.
“For your praise will never depart from the hearts of those who remember the power of God, forever.

May God make these things yours for an everlasting day, and may he show you kindness, because you did not spare your own life when our people were humiliated, but went out because of our downfall and walked uprightly before our God.” And all the people said, “Amen! Amen!”
Judith said to them, “Listen to me, my brothers. Take this head and hang it on the [?] of the wall.

“When morning dawns and the sun rises over the earth, each of you is to take his weapons. Bring every fighting man outside the city and appoint a leader over them. Go out as though to attack the Assyrians’ forward outpost, but do not go down.”

Then they will take up their weapons, go to their camp, and wake their army commanders. They will run to Holofernes’ tent but will not find him. Fear will fall upon them, and they will flee before you.
Then all of you who live within the borders of Israel will go out, strike them down, and leave them lying along the roads.
But before you do this, summon Achior the Ammonite, so that he may see and recognize the one who has restored the house of Israel—the man whom they sent to us as though to his death.
They summoned Achior from Uzziah’s house. When he came and saw Holofernes’ head in a man’s hand in the assembly of the people, he fell on his face and his spirit failed him.
When they took hold of him and raised him up, he fell at Judith’s feet, bowed before her, and said to her, “Blessed are you among every people! They will hear of you and be afraid.
Now tell me everything you have done during these days.” She told him everything she had done, from the day she went out until the day she spoke with them.
When she stopped speaking, the people shouted loudly, and the sound of rejoicing was heard in their city.
When Achior saw everything God had done for Israel, he believed in God, circumcised the flesh of his foreskin, and joined the people of the house of Israel, remaining among them to this day.
When dawn broke, they hung Holofernes’ head outside the wall. Each man took up his weapons, and they went out toward the camp by the ascent into the mountains.
When the Assyrians saw them, they sent word to their leaders, their commanders of thousands, and all their officers.

They went to Holofernes’ tent and said to Bagoas, who was in charge of all his affairs, “Go in and wake our master, because these men have dared to come down against us for battle, only to perish forever.”
Bagoas went and knocked at the entrance of the tent, for he thought that he was sleeping with Judith.
When no one answered him, he opened the entrance and went into the bedchamber. He found Holofernes lying naked, with his head cut off.
He cried out loudly, and with weeping, groaning, and a great outcry, he tore his clothes.
He went into the tent where Judith had been staying but did not find her. He went out to the people and said to them,
“The slaves have betrayed their masters! A single Hebrew woman has brought this disgrace upon the house of Nebuchadnezzar. Look, Holofernes is lying on the ground with his head cut off!”
When the commanders of the Assyrian army heard his words, they tore their tunics, and they were deeply shaken there in the camp.
When those in the tents heard, they wondered what had happened.
Fear and trembling fell upon them. No one stayed beside his neighbor; instead, they turned and fled together along every road through the valleys and mountains.
Those who were encamped in the mountains and the surrounding area also took to flight. Then the Israelites—all their fighting men—attacked them, and they were slaughtered by them.
Uzziah sent messengers throughout all the territory of Israel to tell them what had happened, so that they would all go out against the enemies and destroy them.

When the Israelites heard, they all fell upon them together and kept killing them as far as Choba. So did the people of Jerusalem who came from all the mountain regions, because they had heard everything that had happened to their enemies’ camp. Those in Gilead and Galilee also went out against them and struck them down in a great slaughter until they had passed beyond Damascus and its territory.
The rest of the inhabitants of Bethulia fell upon the Assyrian camps, plundered them, took spoils, and became very rich.
The Israelites returned from battle and took possession of the remaining towns in the mountains and the valley, taking a great deal of plunder.
Joakim the high priest and the elders of Israel who lived in Jerusalem came to greet Judith.
When she came out to them, they all surrounded her together and said, “You are the glory of Jerusalem, the pride of Israel, and the honor of our people!

You have done all these things with your own hands. You have done good things for Israel, and the Lord has been pleased with them. May you be blessed by the Lord Almighty forever and ever.” And all the people said, “Amen.”

The people spent three days clearing out the Assyrians’ camps. They gave Judith Holofernes’ tent, all the furnishings of his tent, his bed, his livestock, and his belongings. She took them and loaded them onto mules; she harnessed her wagons and put the goods in them.
All the women of Israel ran to her and surrounded her. She chose groups of women from among them to sing praises. She took palm branches in her hand and gave them to the women with her.

She put olive wreaths on her head, as did her companion. All the leaders of the house of Israel came, along with all the leading women of Israel. All the Israelites came with them, armed and wearing wreaths, with praise on their lips.
Judith led all Israel in her thanksgiving, and all the people responded with praise to the Lord.
Judith said: Praise the Lord with tambourines; sing to him with cymbals. Sing him a new song of praise; exalt him and call upon his name.
You are the God who crushes wars, the Lord who established a camp among your people to rescue them from the hands of their oppressors.
The Assyrian came from the mountains of the north; he came with the myriads of his army. By their great numbers they blocked the streams, and their horses covered the hills.
They spoke of burning my territories, killing my troops with the sword, dashing infants to the ground, taking children captive, and carrying off my virgins as plunder.
The mighty Lord plundered them; by the hand of a woman he put them to shame.

For their mighty men did not fall at the hands of soldiers, nor did the sons of strong men strike him down, nor did men of towering height fall upon them. Instead, Judith daughter of Merari enticed him with the beauty of her face.
She took off her widow's clothes, for the glory of Israel's sufferings, and anointed her face with perfume.
She bound her braids in a hairnet and put on her clothing to entice him.
Her sandals captured his eyes, and her beauty captivated his soul. [?] cut through his neck.
The Persians trembled at her boldness, and the Medes were shattered by her strength.
Then my humble people shouted, and my weak people cried out, and they fell. They raised their voices and were shattered.
They stabbed them as though they were a young woman, and killed them like rebellious slaves. They perished as though struck by the camp of the Lord our God.
I will sing my God a new song of praise. Mighty Lord, you are great and glorious, a warrior of strength, and you cannot be defeated.

All nations will serve you, and the whole earth, your creation, will submit to you. For you spoke, and they came into being; you set them in order, and they stood firm. There is no one who can stand against your word.
The mountains will shake from their foundations, together with their waters, and the rocks will melt like wax before you. But you will show mercy to those who fear you.
For every sacrifice is too small for an aroma of [?], and all the fat is insufficient for whole burnt offerings. But whoever fears the Lord is great in his sight at all times.

Woe to the nation that rises against my people! The mighty Lord will exact repayment from them. On the day of judgment he will call them to account and punish them. He will give their flesh to fire and worms, and they will cry out in their wickedness forever.
When she came to Jerusalem, they worshiped the Lord. The people purified themselves and continually brought their whole burnt offerings and sacrifices to the Lord.
Judith brought Holofernes' belongings and the canopy she had taken from his bedroom, and dedicated them irrevocably to the Lord.
The people rejoiced in Jerusalem before the sanctuary for a month, and Judith remained with them there in Jerusalem.
After these days, everyone returned to his own dwelling. Judith went to Bethulia, to her own estate, and she was honored throughout the land.
Many desired to marry her, but no man had sexual relations with her for the rest of her life after the death of her husband Manasseh.

As time went on, she grew older, until she reached a very advanced age. She grew old in the house of her husband Manasseh and reached the age of one hundred and five. She died in Bethulia and was buried in the burial caves with her husband Manasseh.

The whole house of Israel mourned her for seven days. Before her death she distributed her possessions among all the relatives of her husband Manasseh and those related to her own family, and she set her female slaves free.
No one again terrified the Israelites throughout Judith's lifetime, or for many days after her death. The book of Judith is finished.
